51212097.DESCRIPTION: Binding affinity to influenza A virus A/WSN/33 (H1N1) Hemagglutinin by surface Plasmon resonance assay
references_previous: Reference [46]: E. Suenaga, H. Mizuno, K.K. Penmetsa, Monitoring influenza hemagglutinin and glycan interactions using surface plasmon resonance, Biosens. Bioelectron. 32 (2012) 195–201.
Reference [47]: J. Yang, M. Li, X. Shen, S. Liu, Influenza A virus entry inhibitors targeting the hemagglutinin, Viruses 5 (2013) 352–373.

Reference [48]: J.L. Ou, Y. Mizushima, S.Y. Wang, D.Y. Chuang, M. Nadar, W.L. Hsu, Structure-activity relationship analysis of curcumin analogues on anti-influenza virus activity, FEBS J. 280 (2013) 5827–5840.

Reference [49]: I.A. Leneva, R.J. Russell, Y.S. Borisikin, A.J. Hay, Characteristics of arbidol-resistant mutants of influenza virus: implications for the mechanism of anti-influenza action of arbidol, Antivir. Res. 81 (2009) 132–140.

original_paragraph.Materials and Methods - Surface plasmon: Interactions between the influenza HA and the compounds were analyzed using the Biacore T200 system (GE Healthcare, Uppsala, Sweden) at 25 °C. Recombinant influenza HA (Sino Biological Inc., Beijing, China) was immobilized on a sensor chip (CM5) using an amine coupling kit (GE Healthcare, Buckinghamshire, UK). Final HA immobilized levels were typically ~16,000 RU. Subsequently, compounds were injected as analyte at various concentrations, and using PBS-P (10 mM phosphate buffer with 2.7 mM KCl and 137 mM NaCl, 0.05% Surfactant P20, pH 4.5) as running buffer. For binding studies, analytes were applied at corresponding concentrations in running buffer at a flow rate of 30 μL/min with a contact time of 60 s and a dissociation time of 60 s. Chip platforms were washed with running buffer and 50% DMSO. Data were analyzed with the Biacore evaluation software (T200 Version 1.0) by curve fitting using a 1:1 binding model. To explore whether 18–HA binding had any effect on interactions between HA and its sialic acid receptor, the sialic acid receptor, the α-2,6 glycan (6′ S-Di-LN: Neu5Aca2-6Galb1-4GlcNAcb1-3[2b-SpNH-LC-LC-Biotin]), kindly provided by the CAS Key Laboratory of Pathogenic Microbiology and Immunology, Institute of Microbiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China and Scripps Research Institute, Department of Molecular Biology, La Jolla, CA, USA, was immobilized on a SA sensor chip with 320 response units. HA protein at 20, 10, 5, 2.5, 1.25, 0.625, or 0 μg/ml flowed through the chip in absence or presence of 18 or other compounds at a flow rate of 10 μL/min with a contact time of 120 s and a dissociation time of 600 s. The sialic acid receptor-SA chip was regenerated with glycine (pH 2.5). The data were analyzed with Biacore evaluation software (T200 Version 1.0) by curve fitting using a 1:1 binding model.
original_paragraph.Figure 10 caption: Fig. 10. The K_D values of compounds reacted with HA protein. (A) Characterization of the affinity between lead compounds (17 and 18) and HA protein, which was immobilized on a CM5 sensor chip, based on the surface Plasmon resonance assay. Their K_D values are labeled in the corresponding curves. (B) The effect of 18–HA binding on interactions between HA and its sialic acid receptor. HA protein flowed across the sialic acid receptor-chip surface in absence or presence of the lead compound (100 μM 18, 100 μM 17, 100 μM Arbidol or 20 μM Curcumin), and lead K_D at 70, 451, 83, 81 and 507 nM. Curcumin was taken as a positive control, while 17 and Arbidol were taken as a negative control.
original_paragraph.SPR Analysis - Text in Results Section: We then characterized the affinity of the active compounds 17 and 18 to HA protein by a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiment. It was found that all these compounds bind to the HA protein immobilized on the CM5 chip, producing dose-dependent responses (Fig. 10A). The calculated K_D value for 18, based on SPR data, was 32 μM, significantly higher than for the weaker inhibitor 17 which exhibited K_D values of 98 μM. Therefore, the affinity of these compounds to HA protein correlated well to their antiviral effects, supporting HA protein as a potential target of 18. Having identified HA as the potential target, we explored whether binding of 18 with HA has any effect on the interaction of HA with its sialic acid receptor, the critical step for attachment of influenza viruses to host cells for initiation of viral infection. According to the SPR assay in which the sialic acid receptor was immobilized on an SA chip, we found, consistent with a previous report [46], that HA protein at concentrations of 0.625–20 μg/ml binds tightly to the sialic acid receptor in a dose-dependent manner with a K_D value of 70 nM (Fig 10B and SI Table 2). When 18 and curcumin, an entry inhibitor targeting the HA1 domain [47,48], are tested in separate assay, the affinity of HA with sialic acid receptor is decreased significantly with K_D values of 541 and 507 nM, respectively. In contrast, arbidol [49], an anti-influenza drug targeting the HA2 domain, has almost no effect on the affinity (K_D 81 nM). Clearly, compound 18 has the same capability as curcumin, potentially targeting the same HA1 domain and blocking the binding of HA to the sialic acid receptor. It seems likely that targeting the HA2 domain has no effect on the interaction of HA with the sialic acid receptor. It was also found that the weaker inhibitor 17 has far less effect (K_D = 83 nM) than 18 on HA-sialic acid receptor interaction, suggesting that the potency of the compound against the influenza virus is directly correlated to the inhibition of the HA-sialic acid receptor interaction.
